sections.heading: How the message generator works
sections.body:
Open the [LinkedIn message generator](https://linkedin-message.lazur.app/) and fill in three fields.

1. Type: choose Connection request, Follow-up, Cold outreach, Thank you or Asking for a referral.
2. Who is it to and why? Write one or two plain sentences. Say who the person is and why you want to reach them.
3. Tone: choose Warm, Professional or Casual.

Run it and you get two different options, each a complete message. They are two drafts, not one text split in half. Read both, pick the one that sounds like you, and change any detail that is not true.

**The answer comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds.** Copy the option you like with one click, then paste it into LinkedIn.

sections.heading: Give the tool a real reason
sections.body:
The only inputs are the type, the who and why, and the tone. If the box says only recruiter, the message will be generic. If it says the person posted about hiring for a data team in Denver, and you work with dashboards every day, the message has something specific to say.

A message that gets answered usually does three things. It says why you picked this person, why you want to connect, and what you hope happens next. Put those three points into the who and why box, and the two options will follow them. Skip flattery, and skip any claim you cannot back up, such as saying you read everything the person has written.

sections.heading: Check the length before you send
sections.body:
LinkedIn's help page says a personal note can be up to 200 characters. Anything longer is more than LinkedIn allows, so cut it down before you paste. The tool is asked to keep connection requests short, but the count is yours to check, so count the option you pick.

The same page says a free account can add a personal note to up to 3 connection requests per month. Premium members are not subject to that monthly cap, though general connection request limits still apply. Save notes for the people where a reason to connect matters most, and send a plain request to the rest.

sections.heading: Where the message goes on LinkedIn
sections.body:
On a computer, LinkedIn's help page lists these steps:

1. Go to the member's profile.
2. In the introduction section, click Connect.
3. Click Add a note.
4. Type your message in the text field.
5. Click Send invitation.

On a phone, the steps are:

1. Go to the member's profile.
2. Tap the More icon at the top of the profile.
3. Tap Personalize Invite.
4. Enter your message.
5. Tap Send Invitation.

Menus change. If a label looks different on your screen, check LinkedIn's help page on personalizing invitations to connect.

sections.heading: What the generator does not do
sections.body:
The generator does not open your LinkedIn account, and it does not send anything for you. You copy the text and paste it yourself. It runs on Lazur's servers with Google Gemini, so the text you type is sent there to write your two options.

If you write LinkedIn messages all day, Lazur on your Mac can type them for you. Hold two keys and talk, and the words land in whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

sections.heading: Examples for common situations
sections.body:
These are sample notes written for this page. Swap in the real name, the real reason and the real detail before you send one. Each one is short enough for LinkedIn's note field.

- **Alumni:** Hi Priya, I also studied at Lakeside State and saw you moved into product design. I am making a similar move, so I would like to learn from your path.
- **Recruiter:** Hi Marcus, I saw your post about hiring analysts for the Denver team. I work with SQL and dashboards every day. Happy to connect and hear what you look for.
- **After an event:** Hi Sam, good talking with you at the logistics meetup on Tuesday. You mentioned a warehouse scheduling problem, and I would like to keep in touch.
- **Peer:** Hi Lena, your article on remote onboarding matched what our team is trying now. I would like to follow your work and compare notes sometime.

sections.heading: What makes each one work
sections.body:
Each sample does the same three things. It names a reason for the message, such as the school, the post, the event or the article. It says why you want to connect. And it asks for something small, or leaves a door open, so the person can reply without a long commitment.

The weakest notes skip the reason. A line that only says you would like to join someone's network tells the person nothing. Name one true detail that fits only this person, and the note already stands out from a generic invite.

faq.q: What is a good LinkedIn connect message?
faq.a: A good connect message names one real reason for reaching out and says what you want, in 200 characters or less. Mention a shared school, a post the person wrote, or an event you both attended. Keep it short and specific, and do not ask for a job or a sale in the first note.

faq.q: How do I message on LinkedIn to connect?
faq.a: On a computer, go to the person's profile, click Connect, click Add a note, type your message, and click Send invitation. On a phone, tap More and then Personalize Invite. LinkedIn's help page says a note can be up to 200 characters, and a free account can add one to up to 3 requests per month.

faq.q: How do you say you want to connect on LinkedIn?
faq.a: Say it plainly in the first line, then give the reason. For example: I would like to connect because we both work on warehouse planning. Then say what you hope for, such as swapping notes, not a meeting. That way the person can say yes without a long commitment.
